claim: Fly song consists of two major modes: sine song and pulse song.

evidence: This describes the structure of fly song, shown in Figure 1A.

The median temporal error for pulse is 0.3 ms which is negligible compared to the average duration of a pulse (5–10 ms) or of a pulse interval (35–45 ms) (Deutsch et al., 2019).

claim: For sine song, the median temporal error for on- and offsets was 12 ms, which is almost half of that of FSS (22 ms).
source: For sine song, the median temporal error for on- and offsets was 12 ms, which is almost half of that of FSS (22 ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing DAS to FSS.

claim: Sine song can have low SNR and fades in and out, making the precise identification of sine song boundaries difficult even for experienced manual annotators.
source: Sine song can have low SNR (Figure 1M) and fades in and out, making the precise identification of sine song boundaries difficult even for experienced manual annotators (see Figure 1A,C).
evidence: This is an observation about the challenges of annotating sine song, illustrated in figures.

claim: Recording song during naturalistic interactions in large behavioral chambers often requires multiple microphones.
source: Recording song during naturalistic interactions in large behavioral chambers often requires multiple microphones (Coen et al., 2014; Neunuebel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: DAS was trained to annotate recordings from a chamber tiled with nine microphones.
source: To demonstrate that DAS can process multi-channel audio, we trained DAS to annotate recordings from a chamber tiled with nine microphones (Coen et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup for testing DAS on multi-channel audio.

claim: DAS processes multi-channel audio by using filters that take into account information from all channels simultaneously.
source: DAS processes multi-channel audio by using filters that take into account information from all channels simultaneously.
evidence: This describes how DAS processes multi-channel audio.

claim: Maximal performance was achieved by training separate networks for the pulse and for the sine song.
source: As is the case for existing methods (Arthur et al., 2013), we achieved maximal performance by training separate networks for the pulse and for the sine song (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: In multi-channel recordings, DAS annotates pulse song with 98% precision and 94% recall, and sine song with 97% precision and 93% recall.
source: In multi-channel recordings, DAS annotates pulse song with 98% precision and 94% recall, and sine song with 97% precision and 93% recall, and matches the performance of FSS (FSS pulse precision/recall 99/92%, sine 95/93%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D–L.

claim: DAS matches the performance of FSS for multi-channel recordings.
source: In multi-channel recordings, DAS annotates pulse song with 98% precision and 94% recall, and sine song with 97% precision and 93% recall, and matches the performance of FSS (FSS pulse precision/recall 99/92%, sine 95/93%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D–L.

claim: Annotations of multi-channel audio have high temporal precision for pulse (DAS 0.3 ms, FSS 0.1 ms) and sine (DAS 8 ms, FSS 15 ms).
source: Annotations of multi-channel audio have high temporal precision for pulse (DAS 0.3 ms, FSS 0.1 ms) and sine (DAS 8 ms, FSS 15 ms) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E,J.

claim: DAS performs better or as well as the current state-of-the-art method for annotating single and multi-channel recordings of fly song.
source: Overall, DAS performs better or as well as the current state-of-the-art method for annotating single and multi-channel recordings of fly song.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented for fly song.

claim: Mice produce ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) in diverse social contexts ranging from courtship to aggression.
source: Mice produce ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) in diverse social contexts ranging from courtship to aggression (Sangiamo et al., 2020; Warren et al., 2020; Neunuebel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: DAS was tested using audio from an intruder assay, in which an anesthetized female was put into the home cage and the USVs produced by a resident female or male were recorded.
source: We tested DAS using audio from an intruder assay, in which an anesthetized female was put into the home cage and the USVs produced by a resident female or male were recorded (Ivanenko et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup for testing DAS on mouse USVs.

claim: The female USVs from this assay typically consist of pure tones with weak harmonics and smooth frequency modulations that are often interrupted by frequency steps.
source: The female USVs from this assay typically consist of pure tones with weak harmonics and smooth frequency modulations that are often interrupted by frequency steps (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This describes the characteristics of female mouse USVs, illustrated in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The male USVs are similar but also contain complex frequency modulations not produced by the females in this assay.
source: The male USVs are similar but also contain complex frequency modulations not produced by the females in this assay (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This describes the characteristics of male mouse USVs, illustrated in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Recording noise from animal movement and interaction as well as the frequency steps often challenge spectral threshold-based annotation methods and tend to produce false positive syllables.
source: Recording noise from animal movement and interaction as well as the frequency steps often challenge spectral threshold-based annotation methods and tend to produce false positive syllables (Tachibana et al., 2020; Coffey et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Weak signals often lead to missed syllables or imprecisely delimited syllables.
source: Moreover, weak signals often lead to missed syllables or imprecisely delimited syllables.
evidence: This is a general statement about challenges in annotating weak signals.

claim: DAS annotates the female USVs with excellent precision (98%) and recall (99%).
source: DAS annotates the female USVs with excellent precision (98%) and recall (99%) (Figure 2E) and low median temporal error (0.3 ms) (Figure 2F).

claim: DAS annotates the female USVs with low median temporal error (0.3 ms).
source: DAS annotates the female USVs with excellent precision (98%) and recall (99%) (Figure 2E) and low median temporal error (0.3 ms) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: DAS is robust to noise: Even for weak signals (SNR 1/16) the recall is 90%.
source: DAS is robust to noise: Even for weak signals (SNR 1/16) the recall is 90% (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: These performance values are on par with that of methods specialized to annotate USVs.
source: These performance values are on par with that of methods specialized to annotate USVs (Tachibana et al., 2020; Coffey et al., 2019; Van Segbroeck et al., 2017) (see Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data shown in Table 3.

claim: USVs of female and male residents have similar characteristics.
source: USVs of female and male residents have similar characteristics (Figure 2A,B) and the female-trained DAS network also accurately annotated the male vocalizations (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is an observation based on the data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The female-trained DAS network also accurately annotated the male vocalizations.
source: USVs of female and male residents have similar characteristics (Figure 2A,B) and the female-trained DAS network also accurately annotated the male vocalizations (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Even the male syllables with characteristics not seen in females in the paradigm were detected.
source: Notably, even the male syllables with characteristics not seen in females in the paradigm were detected (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: DAS accurately and robustly annotates mouse USVs and generalizes across sexes.
source: Overall, DAS accurately and robustly annotates mouse USVs and generalizes across sexes.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented for mouse USVs.

claim: A network was trained to annotate vocalization from pairs of marmosets.

claim: The recordings contain lots of background noises like faint calls from nearby animals, overdrive from very loud calls of the recorded animals, and large variability within syllable types.
source: The recordings contain lots of background noises like faint calls from nearby animals, overdrive from very loud calls of the recorded animals, and large variability within syllable types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the marmoset recordings, illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: A deep-learning-based method was shown to produce good performance (recall 77%, precision 85%, 12.5 ms temporal error) when trained on 16,000 syllables to recognize seven vocalization types.
source: Recently, a deep-learning-based method was shown to produce good performance (recall 77%, precision 85%, 12.5 ms temporal error) when trained on 16,000 syllables to recognize seven vocalization types (Oikarinen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: DAS was trained on 1/9th of the data (1800 syllables) containing four of the seven vocalization types.

claim: Despite the noisy and variable vocalizations, DAS achieves high syllable-wise precision and recall (96%, 92%).
source: Despite the noisy and variable vocalizations, DAS achieves high syllable-wise precision and recall (96%, 92%, (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F)).

source: Note that DAS obtains this higher performance at millisecond resolution (temporal error 4.4 ms, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), while the method by Oikarinen et al., 2019 only produces annotations with a resolution of 50 ms (Table 2).

claim: Bird song is highly diverse and can consist of large, individual-specific repertoires.
source: Bird song is highly diverse and can consist of large, individual-specific repertoires.
evidence: This is a general statement about bird song based on established knowledge.

claim: The spectral complexity and large diversity of the song complicates the annotation of syllable types.
source: The spectral complexity and large diversity of the song complicates the annotation of syllable types.
evidence: This is an inference about the challenges of annotating bird song.

claim: Traditionally, syllable types are annotated based on statistics derived from the segmented syllable spectrogram.
source: Traditionally, syllable types are annotated based on statistics derived from the segmented syllable spectrogram.
evidence: This is a statement about traditional methods for annotating bird song.

claim: Good annotation performance has been achieved with unsupervised methods and deep neural networks.
source: Recently, good annotation performance has been achieved with unsupervised methods (Sainburg et al., 2020; Goffinet et al., 2021) and deep neural networks (Koumura and Okanoya, 2016; Cohen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: DAS was trained to annotate the song from four male Bengalese finches.
source: We first trained DAS to annotate the song from four male Bengalese finches (data and annotations from Nicholson et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup for testing DAS on Bengalese finch song.

claim: The network was tested on a random subset of the recordings from all four individuals which contained 37 of the 48 syllable types from the training set.
source: The network was then tested on a random subset of the recordings from all four individuals which contained 37 of the 48 syllable types from the training set (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup for testing DAS on Bengalese finch song.

claim: DAS annotates the bird song with high accuracy: Sample-wise precision and recall are 97%.
source: DAS annotates the bird song with high accuracy: Sample-wise precision and recall are 97% and syllable on- and offsets are detected with sub-millisecond precision (median temporal error 0.3 ms, Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Syllable on- and offsets are detected with sub-millisecond precision (median temporal error 0.3 ms).
source: DAS annotates the bird song with high accuracy: Sample-wise precision and recall are 97% and syllable on- and offsets are detected with sub-millisecond precision (median temporal error 0.3 ms, Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The types of 98.5% the syllables are correctly annotated, with only 0.3% false positives, 0.2% false negatives, and 1% type confusions.
source: The types of 98.5% the syllables are correctly annotated, with only 0.3% false positives (noise annotated as a syllable), 0.2% false negatives (syllables annotated as noise), and 1% type confusions (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: This results in a low sequence error (corresponding to the minimal number of substitutions, deletions, or insertions required to transform the true sequence of syllables into the inferred one) of 0.012.
source: This results in a low sequence error (corresponding to the minimal number of substitutions, deletions, or insertions required to transform the true sequence of syllables into the inferred one) of 0.012.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: DAS performs as well as specialized deep-learning-based methods for annotating bird song.
source: Overall, DAS performs as well as specialized deep-learning-based methods for annotating bird song (Koumura and Okanoya, 2016; Cohen et al., 2020, Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data shown in Table 2.

claim: A network was trained to annotate song from Zebra finches.
source: To further demonstrate the robustness of DAS, we trained a network to annotate song from Zebra finches.

claim: In Zebra finch males, individual renditions of a given syllable type tend to be more variable.
source: In Zebra finch males, individual renditions of a given syllable type tend to be more variable (Fitch et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The particular recordings used here contain background noise from the bird's movement.
source: Moreover, the particular recordings used here (Goffinet et al., 2021) contain background noise from the bird's movement.
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the Zebra finch recordings used.

claim: Despite the variability and noise, DAS annotates the six syllables from a male's main motif with excellent precision and recall, and low temporal error.
source: Despite the variability and noise, DAS annotates the six syllables from a male's main motif with excellent precision and recall, and low temporal error, demonstrating that DAS is robust to song variability and recording noise (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: DAS is robust to song variability and recording noise.
source: Despite the variability and noise, DAS annotates the six syllables from a male's main motif with excellent precision and recall, and low temporal error, demonstrating that DAS is robust to song variability and recording noise (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: DAS accurately and robustly annotates a wide range of signals—from the pulsatile song pulses of flies to the spectrally complex syllables of mammals and birds.
source: In summary, DAS accurately and robustly annotates a wide range of signals—from the pulsatile song pulses of flies to the spectrally complex syllables of mammals and birds.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: DAS constitutes a universal method for annotating acoustic signals that is as good as or better than methods specialized for particular types of signals.
source: DAS therefore constitutes a universal method for annotating acoustic signals that is as good as or better than methods specialized for particular types of signals (Table 2).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on comparison data shown in Table 2.

claim: To efficiently process large corpora of recordings and to be suitable for closed-loop applications, DAS needs to infer annotations quickly.
source: To efficiently process large corpora of recordings and to be suitable for closed-loop applications, DAS needs to infer annotations quickly.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for DAS to be useful.

claim: Throughput measures the rate at which DAS annotates song and high throughput means that large datasets are processed quickly.
source: Throughput measures the rate at which DAS annotates song and high throughput means that large datasets are processed quickly.
evidence: This is a definition of throughput.

claim: Across the five species tested here, DAS has a throughput of 8-82x realtime on a CPU and of 24-267x on a GPU.
source: Across the five species tested here, DAS has a throughput of 8-82x realtime on a CPU and of 24-267x on a GPU (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A 60 min recording is annotated in less than five minutes on a standard desktop PC and in less than 1.5 minutes using a GPU.
source: This means that a 60 min recording is annotated in less than five minutes on a standard desktop PC and in less than 1.5 minutes using a GPU, making the annotation of large datasets feasible (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–H).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the throughput data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The differences in throughput arise from the different sample rates and network architectures.
source: The differences in throughput arise from the different sample rates and network architectures: The marmoset network is fastest because of a relatively shallow architecture with only 2 TCN blocks and a low sampling rate (44.1 kHz). By contrast, the multi-channel Drosophila networks have the lowest throughput because of multi-channel inputs (9 channels at 10.0 kHz) and a comparatively deep architecture with four TCN blocks (Table 4).
evidence: This is an explanation of the throughput differences based on network design.

claim: Latency corresponds to the time it takes to annotate a single chunk of audio.
source: Throughput and latency depend on the chunk duration—the duration of a recording snippet processed by the network at once—and on the batch size—the number of chunks processed during one call. Larger batches maximize throughput by more effectively exploiting parallel computation in modern CPUs and GPUs and reducing overheads from data transfer to the GPU. This comes at the cost of higher latency, since results are available only after all chunks in a batch have been processed.
evidence: This is a definition of latency and explanation of the tradeoff between throughput and latency.

claim: Latencies are short, between 7 and 15 ms on CPUs and GPUs.
source: Latencies are short, between 7 and 15 ms (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1I–P) on CPUs and GPUs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1I–P.

claim: For fly song, latency can be optimized by reducing chunk size with a minimal impact on accuracy.
source: One network parameter impacting latency is the chunk size—the duration of audio processed at once—and we find that for fly song, latency can be optimized by reducing chunk size with a minimal impact on accuracy (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The low latency of annotation makes DAS well suited for triggering realtime optogenetic or acoustic feedback upon the detection of specific vocalizations.
source: The low latency of annotation makes DAS well suited for triggering realtime optogenetic or acoustic feedback upon the detection of specific vocalizations (Bath et al., 2014; Stowers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference about the suitability of DAS for closed-loop applications, supported by citations.

claim: DAS achieves 3x to 10x higher throughput than existing methods.
source: We find that DAS achieves 3x to 10x higher throughput than existing methods (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data shown in Table 2.

claim: The relatively simple, purely convolutional architecture exploits the parallel processing capabilities of modern CPUs and GPUs.
source: This has three main reasons: First, the relatively simple, purely convolutional architecture exploits the parallel processing capabilities of modern CPUs and GPUs.
evidence: This is an explanation of why DAS is fast.

claim: Fourier or wavelet-like preprocessing steps are integrated into the network and profit from a fast implementation and hardware acceleration.
source: Second, Fourier or wavelet-like preprocessing steps are integrated into the network and profit from a fast implementation and hardware acceleration.
evidence: This is an explanation of why DAS is fast.

claim: For multi-channel data, DAS combines information from all audio channels early, which increases throughput by reducing the data bandwidth.
source: Third, for multi-channel data, DAS combines information from all audio channels early, which increases throughput by reducing the data bandwidth.
evidence: This is an explanation of why DAS is fast for multi-channel data.

claim: DAS annotates audio with high throughput (>8x realtime) and low latency (<15 ms) and is faster than the alternative methods tested here.
source: Overall, DAS annotates audio with high throughput (>8x realtime) and low latency (<15 ms) and is faster than the alternative methods tested here.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the speed benchmarks presented.

claim: The high speed renders DAS suitable for annotating large corpora and for realtime applications without requiring specialized hardware.
source: The high speed renders DAS suitable for annotating large corpora and for realtime applications without requiring specialized hardware.
evidence: This is an inference about the suitability of DAS based on its speed.

claim: To be practical, DAS should achieve high performance with little manual annotation effort.
source: To be practical, DAS should achieve high performance with little manual annotation effort.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for DAS to be practical.

claim: DAS can be efficiently trained using an iterative protocol.
source: We find that DAS can be efficiently trained using an iterative protocol (Pereira et al., 2019, Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 4): Annotate a small set of recordings and train the network for a few epochs; then generate annotations on a larger set of recordings and correct these annotations. Repeat the predict-correct-train cycle on ever larger datasets until performance is satisfactory.
evidence: This describes a training protocol for DAS, illustrated in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: For single-channel recordings of fly song, fewer than 50 pulses and 20 sine songs are needed to reach 90% of the performance achieved with the full data set.
source: For single-channel recordings of fly song, fewer than 50 pulses and 20 sine songs are needed to reach 90% of the performance achieved with the full data set.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: For mouse vocalizations, DAS achieves 90% of its peak performance with fewer than 25 manually annotated syllables.
source: For mouse vocalizations, DAS achieves 90% of its peak performance with fewer than 25 manually annotated syllables.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: For the six syllables from a zebra finch, DAS reaches the 90% threshold with only 48 manually annotated syllables (eight per type).
source: Even for the six syllables from a zebra finch, DAS reaches the 90% threshold with only 48 manually annotated syllables (eight per type).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Manually annotating such small amounts of song for flies, mice, or zebra finches takes less than 5 min.
source: Manually annotating such small amounts of song for flies, mice, or zebra finches takes less than 5 min.
evidence: This is an estimate of the time required for manual annotation.

claim: For the song of Bengalese finches, 1–51 (median 8, mean 17) manual annotations are required per syllable type, with one outlier requiring 200 syllables.
source: Likewise, for the song of Bengalese finches, 1–51 (median 8, mean 17) manual annotations are required per syllable type, with one outlier requiring 200 syllables (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Closer inspection reveals that the outlier results from an annotation error and consists of a mixture of three distinct syllable types.
source: Closer inspection reveals that the outlier results from an annotation error and consists of a mixture of three distinct syllable types (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D–F.

claim: Only 626 manually annotated syllabes (424 without the outlier) are required in total to reach 90% of the test performance of a network trained on >3000 annotated syllables.
source: Even with this outlier, only 626 manually annotated syllabes (424 without) are required in total to reach 90% of the test performance of a network trained on >3000 annotated syllables.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Data requirements are higher for the multi-channel recordings of fly song (270 pulses and sine songs), and for the noisy and variable marmoset data (1610 annotations, 400 per type).
source: Data requirements are higher for the multi-channel recordings of fly song (270 pulses and sine songs), and for the noisy and variable marmoset data (1610 annotations, 400 per type), but even in these cases, the iterative training protocol can reduce the manual annotation work.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: DAS requires small to moderate amounts of data for reaching high performance.
source: Overall, DAS requires small to moderate amounts of data for reaching high performance.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data requirements analysis.

claim: High throughput and small training data sets translate to short training times.
source: High throughput (Figure 4A) and small training data sets (Figure 4D) translate to short training times (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the throughput and data requirements, illustrated in Figure 4E.

claim: The single-channel data sets typically achieve 90% of the performance after less than 10 min of training on a GPU.
source: The single-channel data sets typically achieve 90% of the performance after less than 10 min of training on a GPU.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Training on the full data sets typically finishes in fewer than five hours.
source: Training on the full data sets typically finishes in fewer than five hours.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: DAS can be adapted to novel species in short time and with little manual annotation work.
source: Thus, DAS can be adapted to novel species in short time and with little manual annotation work.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the training time and data requirements analysis.

claim: DAS is a supervised annotation method: It discriminates syllable types that have been manually assigned different labels during training.
source: DAS is a supervised annotation method: It discriminates syllable types that have been manually assigned different labels during training.
evidence: This describes the nature of DAS as a supervised method.

claim: Unsupervised methods can determine in unlabelled data whether syllables fall into distinct types and if so, classify the syllables.
source: By contrast, unsupervised methods can determine in unlabelled data whether syllables fall into distinct types and if so, classify the syllables (Tabler et al., 2017; Coffey et al., 2019; Clemens et al., 2018; Goffinet et al., 2021; Sainburg et al., 2020; Sangiamo et al., 2020; Arthur et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: While DAS does not require large amounts of manual annotations, manual labeling of syllable types can be tedious when differences between syllable types are subtle or when repertoires are large.
source: While DAS does not require large amounts of manual annotations (Figure 4D), manual labeling of syllable types can be tedious when differences between syllable types are subtle (Clemens et al., 2018) or when repertoires are large (Sangiamo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges of manual annotation, supported by citations.

claim: Combining DAS with unsupervised methods facilitates annotation work.
source: In these cases, combining DAS with unsupervised methods facilitates annotation work.
evidence: This is an inference about the benefits of combining DAS with unsupervised methods.

claim: For fly song, DAS was trained to discriminate two major song modes, pulse and sine.
source: For fly song, DAS was trained to discriminate two major song modes, pulse and sine.
evidence: This describes how DAS was trained for fly song.

claim: Mouse USVs do not fall into distinct types.
source: Mouse USVs do not fall into distinct types (Tabler et al., 2017; Goffinet et al., 2021; Sainburg et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: For mouse USVs, unsupervised clustering produces a low-dimensional representation that groups the syllables by the similarity of their spectrograms.
source: In this case, unsupervised clustering produces a low-dimensional representation that groups the syllables by the similarity of their spectrograms (Tabler et al., 2017; Coffey et al., 2019; Sangiamo et al., 2020, Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: For marmosets, unsupervised classification recovers the four manually defined call types.
source: For marmosets, unsupervised classification recovers the four manually defined call types (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: Most call types are split into multiple clusters, and the clusters for trills and twitters tend to separate poorly.
source: However, most call types are split into multiple clusters, and the clusters for trills and twitters tend to separate poorly (Figure 4—figure supplement 3G), which reflects the large variability of the marmoset vocalizations.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3G.

claim: For Zebra finches, the unsupervised method produces a one-to-one mapping between manually defined and unsupervised syllable types.
source: This contrasts with the song of Zebra finches, for which the unsupervised method produces a one-to-one mapping between manually defined and unsupervised syllable types (Goffinet et al., 2021; Sainburg et al., 2020; Figure 5H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and data shown in Figure 5H,I.

claim: For the song of Bengalese finches, the unsupervised classification recovers the manual labeling.
source: For the song of Bengalese finches, the unsupervised classification recovers the manual labeling (Goffinet et al., 2021; Sainburg et al., 2020; Figure 5J,K) and reveals manual annotation errors: For instance, the song syllable that required >200 manual annotations to be annotated correctly by DAS is a mixture of three distinct syllable types (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and data shown in Figure 5J,K and Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–F.

claim: The unsupervised classification reveals manual annotation errors.
source: For the song of Bengalese finches, the unsupervised classification recovers the manual labeling (Goffinet et al., 2021; Sainburg et al., 2020; Figure 5J,K) and reveals manual annotation errors: For instance, the song syllable that required >200 manual annotations to be annotated correctly by DAS is a mixture of three distinct syllable types (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–F.

claim: Unsupervised methods simplify annotation work: DAS can be trained using annotations that do not discriminate between syllable types and the types can be determined post hoc.
source: Overall, unsupervised methods simplify annotation work: DAS can be trained using annotations that do not discriminate between syllable types and the types can be determined post hoc.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the benefits of combining DAS with unsupervised methods.

claim: If distinct types have been established, DAS can be retrained to directly annotate these types using the labels produced by the unsupervised method as training data.
source: If distinct types have been established, DAS can be retrained to directly annotate these types using the labels produced by the unsupervised method as training data.
evidence: This is a statement about how DAS can be used with unsupervised methods.

claim: DAS annotates song in single- and multi-channel recordings from flies, mammals, and birds accurately, robustly, and quickly.
source: We here present Deep Audio Segmenter (DAS), a method for annotating acoustic signals. DAS annotates song in single- and multi-channel recordings from flies (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), mammals ( Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and birds (Figs Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) accurately, robustly, and quickly (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: DAS performs as well as or better than existing methods that were designed for specific types of vocalizations.
source: DAS performs as well as or better than existing methods that were designed for specific types of vocalizations (Koumura and Okanoya, 2016; Cohen et al., 2020; Tachibana et al., 2020; Coffey et al., 2019, Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data shown in Table 2.

claim: DAS performs excellently for signals recorded on single and multiple channels, with different noise levels, and with diverse characteristics.
source: DAS performs excellently for signals recorded on single and multiple channels (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), with different noise levels, and with diverse characteristics.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: DAS is a general method for accurately annotating signals from a wide range of recording setups and species.
source: This suggests that DAS is a general method for accurately annotating signals from a wide range of recording setups and species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Using a user-friendly graphical interface, our method can be optimized for new species without requiring expert knowledge and with little manual annotation work.
source: Using a user-friendly graphical interface, our method can be optimized for new species without requiring expert knowledge and with little manual annotation work (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This describes a feature of DAS, illustrated in Figure 4C–E.

claim: Network performance is robust to changes in the structural parameters of the network, like filter number and duration, or the network depth.
source: Network performance is robust to changes in the structural parameters of the network, like filter number and duration, or the network depth (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: The structural parameters do not need to be finely tuned to obtain a performant network for a new species.
source: Thus, the structural parameters do not need to be finely tuned to obtain a performant network for a new species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the robustness analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: The networks trained using a wide range of signal types constitute good starting points for adapting DAS to novel species.
source: We have trained networks using a wide range of signal types (Table 4) and these networks constitute good starting points for adapting DAS to novel species.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the trained networks.

claim: This makes the automatic annotation and analysis of large corpora of recordings from diverse species widely accessible.
source: This makes the automatic annotation and analysis of large corpora of recordings from diverse species widely accessible.
evidence: This is an inference about the impact of DAS.

claim: In the future, incorporating recent advances in the self-supervised or semi-supervised training of neural networks will likely further reduce data requirements.
source: In the future, incorporating recent advances in the self-supervised or semi-supervised training of neural networks will likely further reduce data requirements (Mathis et al., 2021; Raghu et al., 2019; Devlin et al., 2019; Chen and He, 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future improvements, supported by citations.

claim: These approaches use unlabeled data to produce networks with a general and rich representation of sound features that can then be fine-tuned for particular species or individuals using few annotated samples.
source: These approaches use unlabeled data to produce networks with a general and rich representation of sound features that can then be fine-tuned for particular species or individuals using few annotated samples.
evidence: This is a description of self-supervised and semi-supervised learning approaches.

claim: DAS currently does not work well with recordings in which the signals produced by multiple animals overlap.
source: DAS currently does not work well with recordings in which the signals produced by multiple animals overlap.
evidence: This is a statement about a current limitation of DAS.

claim: In the future, DAS will be extended with methods for multi-speaker speech recognition to robustly annotate vocalizations from animal groups.
source: In the future, DAS will be extended with methods for multi-speaker speech recognition to robustly annotate vocalizations from animal groups.
evidence: This is a statement about planned future work.

claim: The high inference speed allows integration of DAS in closed-loop systems in which song is detected and stimulus playback or optogenetic manipulation is triggered with low latency.
source: Lastly, the high inference speed (Figure 4A,B) allows integration of DAS in closed-loop systems in which song is detected and stimulus playback or optogenetic manipulation is triggered with low latency (Bath et al., 2014; Stowers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference about the suitability of DAS for closed-loop applications, supported by citations.

claim: In combination with realtime pose tracking, DAS provides unique opportunities to tailor optogenetic manipulations to specific behavioral contexts.
source: In combination with realtime pose tracking (Mathis et al., 2018; Pereira et al., 2019; Graving et al., 2019), DAS provides unique opportunities to tailor optogenetic manipulations to specific behavioral contexts, for instance to dissect the neural circuits underlying acoustic communication in interacting animals (Coen et al., 2014; Fortune et al., 2011; Okobi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications, supported by citations.
